# vc-x1-messages v0.3.3

Messages for the vc-x1 family. The open threads are the inbox, the history is the archive.

One shared repo every participant can reach is the only thing the protocol assumes. A thread is
one file, appended by everyone who takes part in it, so reading a conversation is reading one
file, and a search for a message's id returns everything ever said under it. Every member's
`custom.md` points at this file, and taking part means following it, pushes included.

## Terminology

Each term stands alone, a term that relies on another follows it, and a kind of a term sits
under it.

- **Member**: a participant, named by its project's name, `vc-x1`, `iiac-perf`, `zc-ring-x1`.
- **Thread**: one conversation, the file `open/m-<tid>.md` while open and `closed/m-<tid>.md`
  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
  in any open thread.
- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
  eye, since the position already says it.
- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
  the close.
- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
  court until the answer comes.
- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
  Computed from the file alone.
- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

## Specimen

`open/m-41.md`, opened by abc to def and ghi, answered by both, and complete: ghi's line at 1
and def's at 2 are above 0, the line naming them, and abc's `done` at 3 is above 1 and 2, the
lines naming abc. `threads` holds 41 or more. Line 2 has a body, `open/m-41-2.md` beside it,
shown after it.

```
# m-41 hello
- m-41-0 2026-09-09T16:00:00Z from abc to def,ghi hello
- m-41-1 2026-09-09T16:05:42Z from ghi to abc hi
- m-41-2 2026-09-09T16:09:12Z from def to abc [hey, and the cycle that answers it](m-41-2.md)
- m-41-3 2026-09-09T16:12:30Z from abc done
```

````

The cycle landed at
https://github.com/winksaville/def/blob/0123456789ab/TODO.md#feat-the-cycle.

## What changed

- one thing
- another, with the command that shows it:

  ```
  vc-x1 validate --fast
  ```
````

  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
  thread naming the old id.
- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.

## Read Actions

### Read messages

This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.

1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
   thread is the context to read it in.
2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.

A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.

### Find a thread

Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.

- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
  its bodies.
- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.

## Write Actions

Every write runs inside these guards, in order:

- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.

Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.

1. Take ownership.
2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).

### Fetch

1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
   working copy, and that is a write.

### Open a thread

1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
   file when it has one.

### Write a line

Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
the reply links the outcome by sha-link.

1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
   it has one.

### Close a thread

The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
and the close sits in the same commit.

1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.

## What is not here

- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
  cannot disagree with the threads.
- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
  and a reader takes what is there.
- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
  and that is the change it would take.
- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
  participants, and history is the only recourse.
- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
  commit the rules require.
- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.

## Versions

The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.

- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears

  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.

content.content:
## Suffix scheme

The cycle (opening -> commits -> closing, per the [Cycle protocol](../AGENTS.md#cycle-protocol))
encodes each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a
Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is not
a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries neither a
number nor a version (see [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: the commits between
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0` and
starts at `-1` (its first commit). A single-step cycle is one commit, the Close-out, and carries the
bare `X.Y.Z` ([Cycle shape](../AGENTS.md#cycle-shape)). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle
needing no Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0`
step without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its commits between
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the step),
so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference above, every
commit carries a distinct version. The bump is the project's, by its own tool, and `vc-x1` never
writes a version: with `[version] file` and `pattern` in the config it refuses a commit that
leaves the version's line unchanged, and `--same-version` commits it as it is.

## Agent-files version

required, all revised as rungs land. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress` and the

under a program heading, each one deeper):

completes at the rung's landing with the conceptual delta: design points, consequences, deferrals,

the cycle." and completes at close-out with what closing taught, in problem/solution form, or
`_None._`.

A rung is `- N (marker) [<title>](TODO.md#<slug>)` and carries no detail beyond that: the title
links to the rung's subsection. A step is identified by its title (prose.md's

still encodes the stage, but that encoding belongs to the manifest and appears nowhere in prose.

The block is the cycle's only record. A design finding that must outlive the cycle goes into a
`notes/` file by the rung that made it ([Cycle-record](../AGENTS.md#cycle-record)).

Options:

          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

          Log file path (captures all levels)

          Where: a path in the workspace, its root or either repo, or a plain
          repo [default: the current directory]

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace, its root or either repo, or a plain
          repo [default: the current directory]

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

subject. The v0.3.1 draft already allows a positional where it reads one way.

The survey at the opening, 0.85.31: `--scope` is a required flag on 18 commands, every one that
writes, and five more take another required flag, `commit --title --body`, `merge --target
--from`, `move-bookmark --bookmark --target`, `delete-bookmark --bookmark`, and `trailers --range`.
Four clap reads as optional and the command refuses without, `lookup --line`, `clone --from`,
`agent-session --file`, and `cycle plan start --title`.

#### Solution

No command takes a required flag:

- `--scope` stays a flag and gets a default per command, `w` in a dual workspace, `b` for the few
  that act on the workspace whole, `init`, `clone`, `sync`, and `repo delete`, `rename`, and
  `move`, and `p` in a plain repo, where `w` and `b` mean nothing. The scope a command used is
  printed, so a default is never silent, and `-s` names any other.
- A required value becomes a positional, in the order the command reads, `rename CURRENT NEW` the
  pattern: `merge TARGET FROM`, `move-bookmark NAME TARGET`, `delete-bookmark NAME`, `trailers
  RANGE`, `lookup FILE:LINE`, `clone FROM`, `agent-session FILE`, and `cycle plan start TITLE`. The
  old flag is refused naming its positional, as the retired positionals were refused naming their
  flags.
- `commit --title --body` stays as is, two flags.
- The agent-files, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, the README, the scripts, and the acceptance tests follow.

#### Acceptance check

A sweep of every command's `--help`, `vc-x1 --help` walked to its leaves, finds no `--<flag> <V>`
in a usage line, `commit`'s two aside, each retired flag is refused naming its positional, and each
command with a scope run without `-s` prints the scope its default chose, `w`, `b`, or `p` as
above.

#### Deliberation

- `--scope` stays a flag: it is a mode of every command that writes rather than any one command's
  subject, and `-s b` reads as one where a bare `b` would not.
- The scope gets a default (wink, 2026-11-28): `w`, and `b` for a few, `init` named.
  - We think the scope was made required so a write never lands on a repo the user did not name.
    Printing the scope used keeps that seen, and `w` is the side a stray write costs the least on,
    the agent side being covered at the Land anyway, N:1 being valid.
  - The few `b` commands are the agent's pick: those that make, sync, or reshape the workspace
    whole, where `w` alone would leave it half done.
  - Open, wink's: the cycle stages, `cycle plan commit`, `rung commit`, `cycle close`, `cycle
    land`, and `cycle push`. The agent-files' default is `-s b`, a pair per rung, and `w` makes
    the default shape N:1, which loses the per-rung agent history unless `-s b` is typed every
    time. The agent's lean is `b` for them, since in a cycle the pair is the normal case, so the
    rule would read "`w` outside a cycle, `b` inside one".
  - A plain repo defaults to `p`, since there is no other side to name.
- `commit --title --body` stays two flags (wink, 2026-11-28): neither value reads as the command's
  subject over the other.
  - Open, wink's: "both can be optional" was read as a remark, not a change. `commit -r REV` and
    `rung commit` in a cycle already default the title, and `commit` outside one keeps both
    required, as today.
- An agent-files change: AGENTS.md's "Each names its scope, `-s`, as every command that writes
  does" and every `-s` example change with it, so the docs rung adopts the draft `v0.3.1-20`
  locally.
- Two code rungs, not one per command: the scope default is one change in the shared args, and the
  positionals are one pattern applied per command, split by kind so each review is a size that
  reads.

I've updated the continuation notes and opened the cycle on its bookmark, `feat-every-required-argument-is-a-positional`. The plan is written in `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and the ladder in `zTOC.md`. The version is `0.85.32-0`, full validation passed, and nothing is committed or pushed.

**Continuation notes:** I dropped two: the one about the uncommitted `@` (those edits now go into this opening) and the "repo rename landed and published" one (the sync confirmed it). The rest stay, since each still waits on you.

**A survey, to ground the plan:**
- `--scope` is required on 18 commands.
- Five commands take another required flag: `commit`, `merge`, `move-bookmark`, `delete-bookmark` and `trailers`.
- Four look optional in `--help` but refuse to run without their value: `lookup --line`, `clone --from`, `agent-session --file` and `plan start --title`.

**Your two answers, and my thoughts:**
- **A default for `--scope`.** I agree it should stay a flag and get a default. I filled in your "few like init" as the commands that act on the whole workspace: `init`, `clone`, `sync`, and `repo delete`, `rename` and `move` default to both repos. In a plain repo it defaults to `p`, since "work" and "both" mean nothing there. Each command will print the scope it used, so a default is never silent.
  - **Where I'd push back:** the cycle commands (`plan commit`, `rung commit`, `close`, `land`, `push`). The agent-files' default today is a pair of commits per rung. If these default to work-only, every rung commits the work repo alone unless `-s b` is typed. The agent repo then loses its per-rung history, and the Land folds it into one commit (still valid, just coarser). My lean is that these default to both, so the rule reads "work outside a cycle, both inside one". I've recorded this as an open question for you.
- **`--title` and `--body`.** Both stay as flags. I read "both can be optional" as a remark, not a change, since `rung commit` in a cycle and `commit -r` already fill in the title. If you meant `commit` should take neither, say so.

**The ladder, provisional:**
1. feat: a command's scope has a default
2. feat: history commands take their values as positionals (`merge TARGET FROM`, `move-bookmark NAME TARGET`, `delete-bookmark NAME`, `trailers RANGE`)
3. feat: lookup, clone, agent-session, and plan start take positionals
4. docs: the agent-files and docs follow the positionals. This changes AGENTS.md's rule that every command that writes names its scope, so the agent-files version moves to the draft `v0.3.1-20`.

Each retired flag will be refused with a message naming its positional.

**Waiting list:** nothing could be promoted. "vc-x2 is seeded from vc-x1" looks ready, and this is the third opening it has come up at. Promote it or not?

please review

content.text:
I think it's a good idea, and there's already a Todo for it: **bookmark takes create, delete, and move** (`TODO.md:2621`, from 2026-10-30). The older **A hyphenated subcommand becomes a command and a flag** points to it as well. My suggestion is to fold it into this cycle, because rung 2 would otherwise turn `move-bookmark NAME TARGET` into positionals only to rename the command in a later cycle.

**What I'd do:**
- **Replace rung 2** with two rungs:
  - **feat: bookmark takes create, delete, move, and rename**: `bookmark move NAME TARGET`, `bookmark delete NAME`, `bookmark rename OLD NEW` and `bookmark create NAME [REV]`. They are subcommands rather than flags, like `jj bookmark` and `repo delete|rename|move`, because each verb takes different options and so gets its own `--help`. `move-bookmark` and `delete-bookmark` would be refused with a message naming the new form.
  - **feat: merge and trailers take their values as positionals**: the rest of the old rung 2.
- **Add `create`** even though you only listed three verbs, since the existing Todo includes it and it costs little.

**Things to watch:**
- **`rename` is new behavior, not a reshape.** Renaming a bookmark on this machine is easy (`jj bookmark rename` in each repo the scope covers). A published bookmark is harder: on the remote, a rename means pushing the new name and deleting the old one, which counts as a push. I'd keep `rename` local by default, with `--push` for the remote side, and that needs your approval like any push.
- **The old Todo carries a behavior change:** `delete` would stop deleting the bookmark on `origin` too, leaving the remote to `--push`. That changes how a Land cleans up, and that cleanup is written into the agent-files. I'd leave it in the Todo and keep today's delete behavior here, so this cycle stays about the shape of the commands. It's your call, since it is the same code.
- **`commit --no-advance` to `--no-move`**, also in that Todo, I'd leave for later.
- **The docs rung grows:** the Land steps in the agent-files name `delete-bookmark`.

Do you want me to change the ladder this way, and should the bookmark Todo's entry be moved into the record?

/// Where: a path in the workspace for `-s b|w`, its root or
    /// either repo, or the repo itself for `-s p` [default: the
    /// current directory]
    #[arg(short = 'R', long, value_name = "PATH")]
    pub repo: Option<PathBuf>,

    /// Which repos, required: `b|both` makes both commits now,
    /// `w|work` the work half with the agent half left to push,
    /// `a|agent` the agent repo alone, unpaired unless `--covers`, and
    /// `p|por` a plain repo's commit
    #[arg(
        short = 's',
        long,
        value_name = "SCOPE",
        value_parser = repo_scope_parser(&["work", "agent", "both", "por"]),
        required = true,
        help = format!("Which repos, required: {REPO_SCOPE_FORMS}")
    )]
    pub scope: RepoScope,

    /// Commit title, the Conventional Commit line
    #[arg(long, value_name = "STR", required = true)]
    pub title: Option<String>,

    /// Commit body, the problem and its solutions, or @PATH to read
    /// Make the closing a plain commit on the ladder, no merge
    #[arg(long, conflicts_with = "target")]
    pub linear: bool,

    /// Other heads joined, each a parent of the closing after @'s own
    #[arg(long, value_name = "REV", value_delimiter = ',')]
    pub join: Vec<String>,

    #[command(flatten)]
    pub scope: Scope,

    /// The closing's title [default: the cycle title, plus " closing"
    /// on a ladder]
    #[arg(long, value_name = "STR")]
    pub title: Option<String>,

import re
def edit(f, anchor, cmd, dual=None):
    s=open(f).read()
    assert s.count(anchor)==1,(f,anchor)
    indent=re.match(r'\s*',anchor).group(0)
    fn = "scope_or_default" if dual is None else "scope_or_default_dual"
    extra = "" if dual is None else f", &[{dual}]"
    line=f'{indent}let scope = crate::common::{fn}(a.scope.as_ref(), a.repo.as_deref(), "{cmd}"{extra});\n'
    i=s.index(anchor)
    s=s[:i]+line+s[i:]

Rung 1, **feat: a command's scope has a default**, is ready for your review. `-s` is now optional on all 18 commands that took it. Nothing is committed; per your note, it stays uncommitted until you approve it. Full validation passes, and the dev build is installed as `vc-x1-dev 0.85.32-1`.

**How the default works**
- **One shared helper** (`default_repo_scope` and `scope_or_default` in `src/common.rs`). It picks both repos only when the repo you run in, the nearest directory up with `.jj` or `.git`, is the workspace's work repo or its agent repo. Anything else gets `p`: a plain repo, a single-repo workspace, a path that can't be read, or a plain repo sitting inside a workspace's tree. That last case is why it doesn't just look up the workspace root: a bare write from a nested repo would otherwise have hit the outer pair.
- **Where "here" is.** It's `-R`'s path, or the current directory. The exception is `repo delete`, `rename` and `move`, which read it from the workspace path they're given.
- **The cycle commands** already know whether there's an agent repo, so they use that: both if there is one, `p` if not.
- **Never silent.** Whenever `-s` is left out, the command prints `<command>: -s b, the default` (or `-s p`), and every `-s` help line names the default. Checked with `vc-x1-dev sync --dry-run` from both repos, which printed `sync: -s b, the default`.

**Commands that default differently.** The plan said these would get their reason recorded in the rung, and they are:
- `merge` defaults to `w`, because it only accepts `w` or `p`.
- `move-bookmark` defaults to `w`, because `a` and `b` require `--yes`, so a default of both would demand it on every bare move.
- `check desc` refuses `p`, so a bare one outside a dual workspace is still refused, now with its own message about `-s p`.

**Tests**
- A new unit test covers each case above.
- The 10 unit tests and 2 CLI tests that asserted `-s` was required now assert it's optional. The two CLI tests (bare `push` and bare `sync` outside any repo) check that the `p` default's note is printed.

**Files:** the helper is in `src/common.rs`; the rest is the field and help change in each command's file. The rung's notes are written under its heading in `TODO.md`.

file.content:
### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is two plain paragraphs, and the
rung's subsection in the record holds the full account, so the breakdown is written once.

- **The problem**, and it defines any word the title assumes. It is *this commit's*, never the
  cycle's: a body whose problem outruns what the diff resolves is describing something larger than
  the commit.
- **The solution**, opening "Solution:". No bullets, so a `--body` flag cannot mistake it for an
  option.
- **The pointer**, a paragraph of its own, two lines, to the record where it is at that commit:
  `See details in TODO.md:` and the heading exactly as written in `TODO.md`, with no quotes and no
  period, never wrapped, `##### <rung title>` for a work rung, its subsection holding the full
  account, and `### <cycle title>` for a bookend and a single-step cycle
  ([why](rationale.md#commit-description)).
- **A bookend body is a pointer**: an opening or closing commit resolves no problem of its own, so
  its body names the cycle by its title, "Opens the cycle ..." or "Closes the cycle ...", with the
  same pointer after it.

Unchanged by this: no version in title or body, no file list, no deliberation, titles per
[Conventional-commit shape](#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--commit).

### Semicolons

Prose carries no semicolons. A semicolon appears only in code (code spans, fenced code, source
files), where it is syntax rather than prose. The structure a semicolon would have joined is written
explicitly instead:

- **Two claims** take a period, each half standing as its own sentence ("The diff empties. The
  history keeps the record.").
- **A continuation** takes a comma with a conjunction, when one half carries the other's thought
  onward rather than making its own claim.
- **A list hiding in prose** (`A; B; C` inside a sentence or bullet) breaks into sub-bullets so the
  structure shows. List items that themselves contain commas restructure the same way rather than
  separating with semicolons.

    at.

    disruptive as moving it. `create` and `delete` take none, as `delete-bookmark` took none.

2	//! place gave the word a flag, and keeps the positional as a hidden
3	//! argument and refuses it with the flag that replaced it, rather
4	//! than with clap's generic unexpected-argument error. A stale doc or
5	//! a habit is told its own fix.
6	
7	/// The refusal for the old positional `value` on `command`, naming
8	/// `flag`, the spelling that replaced it, with the value in place.
9	pub fn refusal(command: &str, value: &str, flag: &str) -> String {
10	    message(command, &format!("{flag} {value}"))
11	}
12	
13	/// The read commands' retired `[REVISION] [COMMITS]` pair, refused

18	    command: &str,

agent-data/agent-files-v0.3.1-19
## Agent-files version

The agent-files set has a version of its own, apart from the artifact's, so which set an adopter
carries is read from a listing rather than a diff, and an `agent-files` title has a token that is
unique by construction ([Project-declared types](prose.md#project-declared-types),
[why](rationale.md#agent-files-version)).

- **Record**: an empty file, `agent-data/agent-files-vX.Y.Z{-suffix}`, the version its name. `ls
  agent-data` shows it without a read, a bump is a rename, and
  `git log --diff-filter=A -- 'agent-data/agent-files-v*'` lists every version beside the commit
  that introduced it.
- **Spelling**: `vX.Y.Z` everywhere the agent-files version is written, the file name, an
  `agent-files` title, and vc-x1's output, so `agent-files v0.1.0` reads the same in all three. The
  `v` is the name-plus-version pair as cargo prints it (`bar v1.0.0`), and a tool's own banner stays
  bare (`vc-x1 0.82.0`), so a `v` number is the set's and a bare one the artifact's.
- **Proposals bump, adoptions copy**: a proposal cycle bumps it at the opening, advancing per
  [Advancing X.Y.Z](#advancing-xyz-patch-by-default), and its rungs walk the
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme) beside the artifact's version, `-0`, `-1`, then bare at the
  close-out, so a set copied from a draft bookmark says on its face that it is unfinished. An
  adoption copies the source's bare file and bumps nothing.
- **An adoption is a copy and a check**: `vc-x1 agent-files copy --from <src>` takes the set, and
  `vc-x1 agent-files diff --from <src>` is the adoption's last act, exiting zero when the two copies
  are the same and printing the differences the acceptance agreed to when they are not.
- **Named by the proposal**: a version names the text as proposed. An adopter that accepts with
  changes carries them as its diff against that text, and two proposers claiming one number are
  two proposals, the later re-proposing under the next.
- **Which digit**: tend toward the patch digit, kept to one digit and rolled over into the minor.
  We think the minor stays within two digits and major increments when a proposal says so.

content.content:
2366	### trailers
2367	
2368	Rewrite a range of work commits' trailers to what is stamped today ([Cross-repo
2369	Linking](#cross-repo-linking-with-git-trailers)), only their descriptions changing, each tree checked
2370	unchanged. It is how a cycle or a test repo moves to a new protocol, and a Land runs the same pass.
2371	
2372	```bash
2373	vc-x1 trailers --update --range main..@- --dry-run   # print each description, a cycle's
2374	vc-x1 trailers --update --range main..@-             # rewrite them
2375	vc-x1 trailers --update --range ..@- --ignore-immutable  # a whole history, main@origin's included
2376	```
2377	
2378	Each `ochid:` becomes the 12-character change id, an older 8 or 32-character id or a SHA naming one
2379	agent commit being expanded, with `orepo:` stamped above it and any `ocid:` and `pcid:` removed. No
2380	trailer holds a SHA, so the range need not go oldest first and there is no cascade. A commit with no
2381	`ochid:` has no partner to link and is only named in the summary. A trailer naming nothing that
2382	resolves, a `lost` or an old short id, is left as it is, with no guessing. A trailer `vc-x1` does not
2383	stamp is kept, below the ones it does. `--range` is required and taken as written, since no base is
2384	assumed. A commit in jj's `immutable()`, `main@origin` among them, is refused without
2385	`--ignore-immutable`, as jj refuses it, and a mutable one, a cycle's bookmark pushed for a backup
2386	among them, is rewritten.
2387	
2388	### squash
2389	
2390	Continue a rung: fold the working copies into the pair `commit` made. A review's fix in the work
2391	`@` folds into the work commit, and the journal into the agent commit, each keeping its change id,
2392	so both trailers stay right without being touched.
2393	
2394	```
2395	vc-x1 squash -s b                                    # both sides
2396	vc-x1 squash -s w                                    # the work side only, a draft too
2397	vc-x1 squash -s w --ignore-immutable                 # a commit in jj's immutable(), main@origin's
2398	vc-x1 squash -s b --title "feat: ..." --body @tmp/body.md   # and rewrite the descriptions
2399	vc-x1 squash -s p -R ../other                        # a plain repo's @ into its @-
2400	```
2401	
2402	`-s` is required and `-R` optional. The agent side goes by where the partner stands: committed by
2403	`commit -s b`, so the journal folds into it, or pending after `commit -s w`, so the journal already
2404	is the partner and push commits it. A published side goes by where it was published:
2405	
2406	- a draft, a published commit jj counts mutable, a cycle's bookmark pushed for a backup among them,
2407	  is rewritten with a warning, since the cycle is not landed and the next push only moves its
2408	  bookmark: pushing is not what makes a commit history
2409	- a commit in jj's `immutable()`, `main@origin`, tags, and what your `immutable_heads()` adds, is
2410	  history others have, refused without `--ignore-immutable`, as jj refuses it
2411	- a published partner with only the journal to fold is left for push, whose agent half folds it
2412	
2413	A linked partner that is already published is left as it is, the journal staying in `@` for the next
2414	agent commit and its description unchanged, so `--title` then rewrites the work commit alone. An
2415	unpublished linked partner, a Land's agent commit included, takes the fold, since jj keeps the change
2416	id of the commit folded into and the `ochid:` naming it still resolves.
2417	
2418	A work `@-` with no trailer is not a pair's. `--title` with `--body` rewrites the descriptions and
2419	keeps each trailer, the one sanctioned re-describe of a trailer-carrying commit, warned or refused
2420	as a fold is. `--dry-run` prints what it would fold and re-describe, and changes nothing.
2421	
2422	### merge
2423	
2424	Add the sources named to one target commit's parents, after the ones it has, keeping the target's
2425	own change, description, and change id, so its trailer stays right. The target's tree becomes the
2426	merge of all its parents with its own change applied, `jj rebase -r <target> -o <p1> ... -o <s1>
2427	...`. One target, empty or not, and N sources, with no assumption about where either lives: each
2428	`--from` is a revset of one or more commits, a bookmark, `main`, a change id, an earlier merge, a
2429	root, added oldest first. Merging sources one at a time and all at once give the same tree.

### trailers

Rewrite a range of work commits' trailers to what is stamped today ([Cross-repo
Linking](#cross-repo-linking-with-git-trailers)), only their descriptions changing, each tree checked
unchanged. It is how a cycle or a test repo moves to a new protocol, and a Land runs the same pass.

```bash
vc-x1 trailers --update --range main..@- --dry-run   # print each description, a cycle's
vc-x1 trailers --update --range main..@-             # rewrite them
vc-x1 trailers --update --range ..@- --ignore-immutable  # a whole history, main@origin's included
```

Each `ochid:` becomes the 12-character change id, an older 8 or 32-character id or a SHA naming one
agent commit being expanded, with `orepo:` stamped above it and any `ocid:` and `pcid:` removed. No
trailer holds a SHA, so the range need not go oldest first and there is no cascade. A commit with no
`ochid:` has no partner to link and is only named in the summary. A trailer naming nothing that
resolves, a `lost` or an old short id, is left as it is, with no guessing. A trailer `vc-x1` does not
stamp is kept, below the ones it does. `--range` is required and taken as written, since no base is
assumed. A commit in jj's `immutable()`, `main@origin` among them, is refused without
`--ignore-immutable`, as jj refuses it, and a mutable one, a cycle's bookmark pushed for a backup
among them, is rewritten.

### squash

Continue a rung: fold the working copies into the pair `commit` made. A review's fix in the work
`@` folds into the work commit, and the journal into the agent commit, each keeping its change id,
so both trailers stay right without being touched.

```
vc-x1 squash -s b                                    # both sides
vc-x1 squash -s w                                    # the work side only, a draft too
vc-x1 squash -s w --ignore-immutable                 # a commit in jj's immutable(), main@origin's
vc-x1 squash -s b --title "feat: ..." --body @tmp/body.md   # and rewrite the descriptions
vc-x1 squash -s p -R ../other                        # a plain repo's @ into its @-
```

`-s` is required and `-R` optional. The agent side goes by where the partner stands: committed by
`commit -s b`, so the journal folds into it, or pending after `commit -s w`, so the journal already
is the partner and push commits it. A published side goes by where it was published:

- a draft, a published commit jj counts mutable, a cycle's bookmark pushed for a backup among them,
  is rewritten with a warning, since the cycle is not landed and the next push only moves its
  bookmark: pushing is not what makes a commit history
- a commit in jj's `immutable()`, `main@origin`, tags, and what your `immutable_heads()` adds, is
  history others have, refused without `--ignore-immutable`, as jj refuses it
- a published partner with only the journal to fold is left for push, whose agent half folds it

A linked partner that is already published is left as it is, the journal staying in `@` for the next
agent commit and its description unchanged, so `--title` then rewrites the work commit alone. An
unpublished linked partner, a Land's agent commit included, takes the fold, since jj keeps the change
id of the commit folded into and the `ochid:` naming it still resolves.

A work `@-` with no trailer is not a pair's. `--title` with `--body` rewrites the descriptions and
keeps each trailer, the one sanctioned re-describe of a trailer-carrying commit, warned or refused
as a fold is. `--dry-run` prints what it would fold and re-describe, and changes nothing.

### merge

Add the sources named to one target commit's parents, after the ones it has, keeping the target's
own change, description, and change id, so its trailer stays right. The target's tree becomes the
merge of all its parents with its own change applied, `jj rebase -r <target> -o <p1> ... -o <s1>
...`. One target, empty or not, and N sources, with no assumption about where either lives: each
`--from` is a revset of one or more commits, a bookmark, `main`, a change id, an earlier merge, a
root, added oldest first. Merging sources one at a time and all at once give the same tree.

```
vc-x1 merge -s w --target @ --from A --from B          # two lines of work into @
vc-x1 merge -s w --target @ --from C                   # one more, after A and B
vc-x1 merge -s w --target X --from 'bookmarks(glob:"f-*")'  # every bookmark matching, at once
vc-x1 merge -s w --target @ --from main --dry-run      # say what it would do
```

`-s`, `--target`, and `--from` are required, `-s` being `w` or `p`, since the agent repo never
holds a merge. A source that is already a parent is skipped, and a merge adding nothing changes
nothing. Removing a parent is not a merge: `jj undo` takes back the last one, and `jj rebase -r
<target> -o ...` sets any parents. Refused: a source that is the target or below it, a cycle, and
a target in jj's `immutable()`, under jj's aliases and yours, unless `--ignore-immutable`, as `jj`
refuses it. A rung pushed to its cycle bookmark is mutable to jj, and the push after its rewrite
takes approval like any other. Reported and allowed: a conflicted result, left as jj leaves it
with `jj resolve --list` named. A source that is an ancestor of another, `main` below the last
rung, is the no-fast-forward shape a closing is, so it is neither refused nor reported.

### move-bookmark

Point one existing local bookmark at one commit, `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <target>`, the
repositioning a bookmark needs before it is pushed, since `push` only sets the line's bookmark to
`@-`. Nothing is pushed.

```
vc-x1 move-bookmark -s w --bookmark feature --target @-       # forward to the last commit
vc-x1 move-bookmark -s w --bookmark main --target feature     # main to where feature is
vc-x1 move-bookmark -s w --bookmark feature --target X --allow-backwards  # off its line
vc-x1 move-bookmark -s w --bookmark feature --target @- --dry-run         # say what it would do
vc-x1 move-bookmark -s b --bookmark main --target @- --yes                # main in both repos
vc-x1 move-bookmark -s p -R ../other --bookmark main --target @-          # any repo, unchecked
```

`-s`, `--bookmark`, and `--target` are required. `-s w` moves the work repo's bookmark. `-s a`, the
agent repo, and `-s b`, both, take `--yes`, since the agent repo's `main` is otherwise set by push's
agent half: the same name in each, the target resolved in each, and every repo checked before any
moves. `-s p` takes the repo from `-R`, required, as it is, with none of the workspace's checks, so
it moves a bookmark in either side of a dual workspace or any jj repo, and careful use is yours.
The bookmark must already exist, none being created, and the target is a revset of exactly one
commit, a bookmark or a rev. A move backward or sideways, leaving
commits off the bookmark's line, is refused unless `--allow-backwards`, as `jj` refuses it, and a
bookmark already at the target is left as it is.

### delete-bookmark

Delete one bookmark locally and on `origin`, the disposal a cycle's bookmark gets at Land, `jj
bookmark delete` and its push in one invocation. The remote goes first, so a failed push leaves the
local bookmark, and a side already gone is no error, so a rerun finishes the job. The commits stay,
and the commit the bookmark was at is printed so it can be recreated.

```bash
vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s w --bookmark feat-a-cycle                # local and on origin
vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s w --bookmark feat-a-cycle --skip local   # origin only
vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s w --bookmark feat-a-cycle --skip remote  # local only
vc-x1 delete-bookmark -s p -R ../other --bookmark old --dry-run   # print, delete nothing
```

`-s` is required: `w` the work repo, `a` the agent repo, `b` both, and `p` the repo `-R` names, as
it is.

### push

Publish a rung's pair, or a name for a commit already made. Push carries no description and writes
none, so what was reviewed is what goes out: `commit` makes the pair and pushes it unless told not
to, and push publishes one it kept local, completing the agent half as its partner.

`-r` is the commit to publish, the work `@-` when left out, and
`--bookmark` is its name on the remote, so the commit and its name are never one word read two
ways, as jj keeps them apart in `jj bookmark set NAME -r REV`. At `@-` the pair goes out on the
line's bookmark, or the one named, a new name created at `@-` and pushed tracked. Any other `-r`
is a commit already made, and a name alone goes out for it, no pair: the one bookmark at it, or
`--bookmark`'s, that bookmark or a new one created there.

```bash
vc-x1 push -s b                        # the pair, on the bookmark the work @- sits on
vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark feature     # the same, the bookmark named as a check
vc-x1 push -s b --bookmark topic       # the pair on a new name, created at @- and pushed tracked
vc-x1 push -s b -r side                # a bookmark off the line, on a commit made, published where it is
vc-x1 push -s b -r xyz --bookmark name # a new name for a commit made, created there and pushed
vc-x1 push -s w                        # the work half only
vc-x1 push -s a                        # the agent half only, the remainder of a run that stopped
vc-x1 push -s p -R ../other            # a plain repo's @- on its bookmark, no trailer asked for
vc-x1 push -s b --dry-run              # plan and print, move nothing
```

Push publishes the work `@-`, so new work in `@`, the next rung started, is left as it is, and
push says so. What push refuses, with both repos as they were:

- a work `@-` with no `ochid:` trailer: not a pair's commit, so `commit` makes one first
- two bookmarks on the line and none named, or a named one not on the line
- a `-r` of several commits, the working copy, which `commit` turns into a commit, or the root,
  which has nothing to publish, and a `-r` with no bookmark at it and none named, or with a
  `--bookmark` that is elsewhere, which `move-bookmark` moves
- `-r` with `-s a`, the agent half publishing the agent `main`
- the old positional, naming `--bookmark` or `-r`, the one it was

### lookup

Show the lines in the other repo that a line in this one relates to. `vc-x1 lookup [-s SCOPE]
--line FILE:LINE` takes a line as an editor, a compiler, or grep prints it, places the file on one
side of the workspace, and resolves it to the window on the other side, work-to-transcript or
transcript-to-work. The requirements are in [What the lookup command
needs](notes/transcript-write.md#what-the-lookup-command-needs).

- `-s`/`--scope` is the side the line is on, `work` or `agent`. Omitted, it is inferred from the
  file's path. Named, a `FILE` that does not exist relative to the current directory is taken
  relative to that side's repo root, so a repo-relative path works from anywhere once the side is
  said. A named side the path disagrees with is an error, never a hint.
- `--line FILE:LINE` splits at its last colon, so a path holding a colon still parses, and the line
  must exist in the file on disk. The old `[SCOPE] FILE:LINE` positionals are refused, naming `-s`
  and `--line`.
- The workspace is `-R`/`--repo` when given, else found from the file.
- `-r`/`--revision REV` reads the line from the file as of REV instead of from disk, for a line
  the working copy no longer holds, such as a cycle-record line the next opening deleted.

A work line prints the commit it arrived in, blamed at the working copy after a snapshot, and
# A plain repo, no agent repo

vc-x1 clone https://github.com/owner/my-project --dry-run

content.content:
### agent-session

Display a Claude Code session transcript (`.claude/<uuid>.jsonl`) as a readable conversation. The
transcript format is undocumented and evolves, so parsing is tolerant: unknown entry types are
skipped and counted, and malformed lines (e.g. a live session's truncated last line) warn to
stderr and never
fail the run.

For what the transcript format looks like (entries, entry types, the `.`/`[]` field notation) and an
example that walks a small sample through these commands, see
[notes/transcript-format.md](notes/transcript-format.md).

Output is composed of eight **items**, each independently toggleable:

| Item | Emits | Default |
|------|-------|---------|
| `summary` | trailing stats line (shown / hidden / skipped counts) | on |
| `headers` | `=== role 2026-07-17 04:17:09Z ===` turn headers (UTC) | on |
| `user` | typed user prompts | on |
```

```
# Default conversation view
vc-x1 agent-session .claude/<uuid>.jsonl

# Everything: thinking, tool results, meta/system too
vc-x1 agent-session --all F

# Prompts only: what was asked, nothing else
vc-x1 agent-session --none --user F

# Default view minus tool calls and headers
vc-x1 agent-session --no-tool --no-headers F

# Slices by source JSONL line (same unit in every view)
vc-x1 agent-session --lines 40 F      # first 40 source lines
vc-x1 agent-session --lines -15 F     # last 15 source lines
vc-x1 agent-session --lines 100,20 F  # 20 lines from Index 100
vc-x1 agent-session --lines 100,-20 F # 20 lines ending at Index 100
vc-x1 agent-session --lines 0 F       # stats summary only
```

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--<item>` / `--no-<item>` | Add / remove one of the eight items (last one wins) |
| `--all` / `--none` | Base: every item on / off (aliases `--no-none` / `--no-all`) |

content.content:
### Committing vs pushing

A local commit can be reworked and a push cannot easily be taken back, so the safe act is the one done
by doing nothing, and publishing has one place to gate.

#### A cycle is local by default

Local is the default because the Land is where the decision is, so one approval belongs there.
Nothing published can name a rung, so reshaping a ladder costs nothing, and a link names a change
id, which a reshape keeps. The first cycle run this way changed its ladder several times at no cost.

**The user decides when each side commits and publishes** (wink, 2026-11-03) because the user is
always in control: the per-rung pairs came first, the local cycle after, and neither is the only
shape, so the rules say what each shape needs rather than choosing one.

**A rung commits as a pair** (wink, 2026-11-09) because nothing now needs the agent-repo still.
While `ocid:` pinned the agent commit's SHA, a work commit could name it only once that SHA was
final, so one agent commit a cycle, made at the Land, was the obvious shape. With change ids that
holds no longer, and a pair per rung keeps each rung's transcript beside its work, one `ochid:`
away, and splits a cycle's transcript rung by rung rather than into one large commit.

**No trailer holds a SHA** (wink, 2026-11-09) because a SHA changes with every rewrite. `ocid:`
pinned the agent commit's, so an agent commit was never folded into and the order of commits was
forced, and `pcid:` repeated git's parents and made a describe rewrite every commit above it.
Neither repo could be left clean. `orepo:` with `ochid:` says where the partner is and survives a
squash-push. Lost: GitHub's one click to the agent commit, and the transcript pinned by a hash.

### Commit description

No version in title or body because a version is stable only once it lands, and a history rewrite
can renumber it. No file list because the diff is the mechanical record. No deliberation because the

Rungs 1 through 5 are committed, so everything up to the closing is done. All of it is still local on `feat-every-required-argument-is-a-positional`: nothing pushed, the closing not started, nothing landed. Full validation passed before every commit, and `vc-x1-dev 0.85.32-5` is installed from the last commit. I recorded your "continue up to the closing" as a waiver in the cycle's record, covering only these rung commits, so your review comes before the closing.

**Rung 1 – the scope default:** committed as you approved it.

I've dropped "vc-x2 is seeded from vc-x1" from `## Waiting` in `TODO.md`, along with the continuation note that kept asking about it. It's uncommitted and will go into the next commit.

**`trailers update RANGE`:** agreed. It's the same shape as `bookmark` and `repo`. `--update` would be refused with a message naming the new form, and since `--range` was retired an hour ago, I'd skip the in-between form and refuse both old flags.

**What "delete no longer deleting on origin" means.** It isn't about `main` versus `main@origin`, and the remote copy still gets deleted. The change is whether that takes an explicit `--push`:
- **Today:** `bookmark delete X` deletes X locally and also pushes the deletion of `X@origin`, all in one command. That's the only bookmark verb that changes the remote without being asked.
- **Proposed:** `bookmark delete X` deletes only the local X. `bookmark delete X --push` also deletes `X@origin`, and `--push --skip local` deletes only the remote one.

The old Todo's reasoning is a rule from the v0.3.1 draft: only a push publishes. Deleting a bookmark on origin is a publish, and the rules say every publish needs its own approval. A verb that publishes without any `--push` on the line makes that easy to miss, for you reading a command or for me typing one.

It also makes the four verbs consistent: `create` and `move` are local, and `rename` is local unless `--push`. With the change, `delete` follows the same pattern.

There's one cost. The Land's own cleanup calls the delete code directly, so it wouldn't change. But the agent-files' Land step 4 (`bookmark delete <bm> -s w --skip local`, which deletes the remote copy only) would become `bookmark delete <bm> --push --skip local`.

My recommendation is to do it, now that the verbs exist.

Both are inside this cycle's subject, so I'd add them as two rungs before the closing, then let the closing put back only `commit --no-advance` → `--no-move` as a Todo:
- **feat: trailers takes update RANGE**
- **feat: bookmark delete reaches origin only with --push** (agent-files step updated too)

Do you want them as rungs in this cycle, or as Todos for a later one? If rungs: should I run them the same way as before (committed locally, your review before the closing), or stop for your review after each?

content.text:
You're right, the Land doesn't need `--skip local`. By step 4, `cycle land` has already deleted the local bookmark, and `delete` treats a side that's already gone as no error. So `bookmark delete <bm> --push` deletes the remote copy and finds nothing left locally. `--skip local` was only a guard that changed nothing there.

With your default, `--skip` loses most of its point:
- `--skip remote` (local only) becomes the plain `delete`.
- `--skip local` (remote only, keeping the local bookmark) is the one case left, for unpublishing a bookmark while you keep working on it. I don't know of anything here that uses it.

So I'd drop `--skip` and keep `delete X` (local) and `delete X --push` (local and origin). A remote-only option can come back if a real need shows up. A `--skip` someone types would be refused with a message naming the new forms. The Land keeps its own internal "which side" handling, since it calls the code directly rather than through the CLI. Step 4 in `agent-data/jj.md` becomes `vc-x1 bookmark delete <bookmark> --push`.

The two rungs would then be:
- **feat: trailers takes update RANGE**
- **feat: bookmark delete reaches origin only with --push**: drops `--skip`, and updates the agent-files and README.

rebase or a fold:

vc-x1 trailers --update
vc-x1 push -s b
```

Every `ochid` on a commit is checked, in any form. An `orepo` is checked too, offline, from the two
repos and what they know of their remotes, and one naming the wrong repo is an `err` that [`trailers
--update`](#trailers) repairs: it must name the other repo's `origin`. A work commit whose agent
partner is committed but not yet on a remote is a `note`, not an error, since that is normal before
### trailers

Rewrite a range of work commits' trailers to what is stamped today ([Cross-repo
Linking](#cross-repo-linking-with-git-trailers)), only their descriptions changing, each tree checked
unchanged. It is how a cycle or a test repo moves to a new protocol, and a Land runs the same pass.

```bash
vc-x1 trailers update main..@- --dry-run   # print each description, a cycle's
vc-x1 trailers update main..@-             # rewrite them
vc-x1 trailers update ..@- --ignore-immutable  # a whole history, main@origin's included
```

Each `ochid:` becomes the 12-character change id, an older 8 or 32-character id or a SHA naming one
agent commit being expanded, with `orepo:` stamped above it and any `ocid:` and `pcid:` removed. No
trailer holds a SHA, so the range need not go oldest first and there is no cascade. A commit with no
`ochid:` has no partner to link and is only named in the summary. A trailer naming nothing that
resolves, a `lost` or an old short id, is left as it is, with no guessing. A trailer `vc-x1` does not
stamp is kept, below the ones it does. The range, RANGE, is required and taken as written, since no
base is assumed, and the retired `--range` is refused naming it. A commit in jj's `immutable()`,
`main@origin` among them, is refused without `--ignore-immutable`, as jj refuses it, and a mutable
one, a cycle's bookmark pushed for a backup among them, is rewritten.

content.content:
# Agent-files size

The line count of the agent-files, one row per landing that changed them, so the set's size is
tracked over time. A cycle that leaves the agent-files untouched adds no row, since a row saying
the count did not move records nothing. Smaller is the quasi-goal: a rule stated once is shorter
than a rule stated three times, and a shrinking count is evidence the set is converging, while a
growing one is a prompt to ask what arrived as a paragraph that should have been a line. The count
is not a rule, and a rule is never cut to move it.

A finding from the proposal cycle (2026-08-27), for whoever next tries a cut: a draft that cut
AGENTS.md from 370 to 320 lines with every rule kept found that the remaining bulk is the rules
themselves, so a further cut has to cut rules, and that is a convention decision, not an edit.

The count is `wc -l` over `AGENTS.md`, `custom.md`, and `agent-data/*.md`, the total leaving out
`rationale.md`, taken at the close-out of a cycle that changed an agent-file and recorded here as
the closing rung's last edit, with the cycle title as the row's label. `rationale.md` is out of the
total because it is the rules' why and grows with every rule that gains one, so a rule gaining a
why does not read as the set growing. Rows before v0.2.5 counted it.

`vc-x1 agent-files size` takes the count and slides the per-file table, a new leftmost column in
and the oldest out. It is dry-run by default and `--no-dry-run` writes the file, `--label=TEXT`
names a column the set's version file cannot, and the `## Counts` row above stays a hand's work,
since its note is prose.

## Counts

| Landed | Cycle | Files | Lines | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-08-25 | docs: the family agent-files proposal opening | 10 | 2205 | vc-x1's set |
| 2026-08-27 | docs: sync the agent-files to zc-ring-x1's set | 12 | 2822 | two files back, 863 |
vc-x1-dev 0.85.32-7+5ad3078f31b2

Count the set's markdown, AGENTS.md, custom.md, and
agent-data/*.md, one line per file and a total. The version
marker is not markdown, so it takes no row and no place in
the file count. It is empty, so it would add nothing to the
total either.
agent-data/rationale.md is: its number is shown in angle
brackets and left out of the total, being the rules' why
rather than a rule.

Then the per-file table in notes/agent-files-size.md, the one
headed `| File |`, gets a new leftmost column labelled by the
set's version file and loses its rightmost one, so the window
keeps its width. Dry-run by default: --no-dry-run writes it.
DIR defaults to this workspace, --file names another notes
file, and --label names a column the version file cannot,
written --label=TEXT when the label opens on a `-`.

Usage: vc-x1-dev agent-files size [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --dir <DIR>
          A directory holding a copy of the set [default: this workspace]

  are `gh repo delete`'s, delete never touching a URL remote.

The extra line comes from one rule in `AGENTS.md`, under **Committing vs pushing**. It used to say each command "names its scope, `-s`", which took 2 lines. The new wording has to say two more things, which took 3 lines:
- `-s` now has a default: `b` in a dual workspace, `p` in a plain repo.
- The agent still types it anyway, so every command in the transcript shows its shape.

The other two `AGENTS.md` edits only swapped words in place (`cycle plan start "<title>"` and `bookmark delete`), so their line counts didn't change. No other file counted in the total changed size. `rationale.md` grew by 6 lines for the new rule's reasoning, but it's left out of the total.

If you want the 2 lines back, a tighter wording fits:

```
  machine and need no approval. Each takes a scope, `-s`, `b` by default in a dual workspace and
  `p` in a plain repo, which the agent names anyway: `b` the pair, `w` the work half, `p` a plain repo.
```

It drops "as every command that writes does" (rung 1 already covers that) and "so the shape is in the command" (the reasoning in `rationale.md` says it). Want me to use it?

content.text:
Confirmed: both names resolve to the same repo (id `1475077277`). So `t31-gh-pub2.agent-session` is just the redirect GitHub kept when that repo was renamed to `.agentsession` earlier. Nothing else holds the name. Renaming a repo back to its earlier name is a normal GitHub operation and replaces the redirect.

**The bug:** `check_github` in `src/repo/rename.rs` asks for the new name, and any answer at all counts as "taken". It should only count as taken when the answer *is* the new name. An answer that is the repo being renamed is its own redirect, so the name is free.
- **The fix:** treat that case as free, and have the plan say that the redirect gets replaced.
- **A related edge:** a redirect that points to a *different* repo is also not a real holder, but renaming over it would break that repo's old links. I'd keep refusing that one, with a clearer message: "a redirect left when X was renamed".
- **Test:** the existing fake GitHub handles this case directly, e.g. `("o/new", "o/old")`.

**To unblock your test now:** GitHub allows the rename, and `repo rename` already continues a run whose GitHub step is done. So:

```
gh repo rename t31-gh-pub2.agent-session --repo winksaville/t31-gh-pub2.agentsession --yes
vc-x1 repo rename t31-gh-pub2/.agentsession .agent-session -s a
```

The second command sees that the repo is already under its new name, marks that step done, and does the rest.

The fix is new work, so it needs its own cycle. One thing first: your local `main` holds the cycle we just landed, which isn't published. A new cycle would branch from that unpublished `main`, which works, but it means the sync at the opening reports `main` as ahead of origin.

How do you want to proceed?
1. Open the cycle **fix: repo rename takes back a name its own redirect holds** now, on top of the unpublished `main`.
2. You run `vc-x1 squash-push -s b` first, then I open it.
3. File it as a Todo for later.

content.text:
I think it works, and it's an option the protocol already names: close-out step 7 lists "fix inside the closing" as one way back from a fault. Some things to weigh.

**What makes it work**
- **Everything is still local.** The closing commit is `main`'s tip, unpublished, so folding into it rewrites nothing anyone else has. `vc-x1 squash -s b` (it's `-s b`; there is no `--both`) folds the work `@` into the closing and the session into the agent's closing commit. Both keep their change ids, so the trailers stay valid. jj moves `main` along with the rewritten commit.
- **It repeats cleanly.** Each fix your testing turns up is one more fold into the same commit, and the closing stays one commit however many fixes land in it.

**What to watch**
1. **It bends a rule.** The rule says "development is never done on `main`", and the closing is already landed on `main`, so folding a fix into it is development on `main`. Your word covers it, but the rules want the bend recorded in the record, saying what it covers (folds into the closing while unpublished) and what it doesn't (the publish). If you'd rather not bend it, the compliant version costs two moves: put `main` back at `5a65776`, recreate the cycle bookmark at the closing, fold the fixes there, then run `cycle land` again.
2. **The bug belongs to a different cycle.** It's in **feat: repo rename renames a workspace**, which is published and closed.
